The music of 1980s home computers and game consoles wasn't recorded. A small **sound chip** played it
live, note by note, as the game ran. The Nintendo Entertainment System (NES, 1983 in Japan as the
Famicom) had **two pulse waves, one triangle wave and one noise channel**, plus a channel for short,
low-quality samples that most games barely used. The Game Boy had nearly the same four: two pulses, a
small wave channel of your own design, and noise. The Commodore 64's SID chip had three voices.

Each channel could play **one note at a time**. That's four notes in all, and one of them is noise,
so it can't hold a pitch. Composers such as Koji Kondo (*Super Mario Bros.*, 1985), Hirokazu Tanaka,
Tim Follin, and on the Commodore 64 Rob Hubbard and Martin Galway still wrote full arrangements:
melody, harmony, bass and drums. The music people now call **chiptune** grew out of the tricks they
used to do it.

**How to use the page.** Press ▶ to hear a four-bar tune written for the four channels. The buttons
mute and unmute each channel. Hold two or three keys (computer keys, the keyboard below, or MIDI) and
the chord channel arpeggiates your chord in place of the song's. Start with the volume low.

## Four channels

<div class="sk" data-w="chip"></div>

Every channel has a job, and the jobs follow from what each channel can do:

| Channel | What it can do | What composers gave it |
|---|---|---|
| **Pulse 1** | a pulse wave at 12.5%, 25% or 50% width, 16 volume levels | the melody |
| **Pulse 2** | the same | harmony, a counter-melody, or an echo of the melody |
| **Triangle** | a triangle wave, an octave lower than the pulses, **no volume control**: on or off | the bass |
| **Noise** | noise, high or low, 16 volume levels | the drums |

The **pulse width** is the instrument choice. 50% is the hollow square wave (odd harmonics only;
[Sound 2](sound-waveforms.qmd)). 25% is fuller and more nasal, and 12.5% is thin and buzzy. Try
both pulse widths while the tune plays. Composers often changed the width partway through a note to
give it more movement.

Because the triangle has no volume control, chip bass lines never fade. A note sounds at full level
until it's cut off, so bass lines are written as bouncing octaves or with short gaps to make the
rhythm. Drums are short bursts of noise: a low, quick one for the kick, a brighter one for the
snare, a tiny high one for the hi-hat (built the same way as in [Sound 3](sound-noise.qmd)). Mute the
other three channels to hear how little each drum is.

## Rows and frames

The music was played by a small program that ran once every screen refresh: **60 times a second**
on American and Japanese machines (50 in Europe). Each run is a **frame**. Nothing in the music
could happen between frames, so every note change, volume step and vibrato wobble fell on a
1/60-second grid.

Composers wrote in **trackers**: a spreadsheet of notes, one column per channel, read from top to
bottom. Each line is a **row**, and the "speed" is how many frames a row lasts. Six frames a row,
with four rows to a beat, gives 150 beats per minute. Tempo only comes in steps: move **Frames per row**
and the tempo jumps between fixed values. Some composers alternated two speeds from row to row to
get a tempo in between.

The program also made the expressive details by hand. The melody's volume steps down frame by frame
after each attack (you can see the steps in the oscilloscope), and after a long note has sounded for
a while its pitch starts to wobble. That's **vibrato**, written in software. Turn it off to hear
how flat the long notes sound without it.

## Chords from one channel

With one channel for the melody, one for the bass and one for drums, only **one channel is left for
harmony**. One channel can play one note. A chord needs at least three.

The answer was the **arpeggio**: play the chord's notes one after another, so fast that the ear
can't hear them as separate notes. Played every frame or every other frame, that's **30 to 60 notes
a second**. Below about 50 ms per note, the ear stops following a tune and hears a texture
instead: a buzzing, shimmering chord. It's the most recognisable chiptune sound.

Compare the three settings of **Chords on pulse 2**:

- **Arpeggio (one channel)**: what the composers actually did.
- **Root only**: what you'd get from that channel without the trick. The harmony is gone, and the
  F and C bars sound like they're missing something.
- **Real chord (three channels)**: what the chip couldn't do. It's smoother, but now three
  channels are busy with one chord and there's nothing left for the tune or drums.

Then go back to *Arpeggio* and slow it down with **Frames per arpeggio note**. At 12 or 15 frames a note you hear a tune of single notes going up and down. Speed
it back up and somewhere around 4 to 6 frames the separate notes merge into a chord. The *pattern*
matters less at full speed: *Up*, *Up and down* and *Up, then the octave* all sound like the same
chord, each with a slightly different buzz.

In trackers this became a one-line effect: `047` on a note means "add 4 and then 7 semitones above
it, each for one frame, over and over": a major chord on one channel. `037` is minor.

## Write your own: a tracker

This is the same tune in a **tracker**, laid out the way chip composers wrote it. Each column is a
channel, each line is a row, and time runs down the page. The shaded lines are beats, and the darker
ones start a bar. Press ▶ and edit while it plays: a change is heard the next time that row comes round.

<div class="sk" data-w="tracker"></div>

What to type in a cell:

| Column | Type | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Pulse 1**, **Triangle** | a note: letter, `-` or `#`, octave | `A-4`, `C#5` |
| **Pulse 2** | a note, then an arpeggio effect `0xy` | `A-4 037` (minor), `C-5 047` (major) |
| **Noise** | `K` kick, `S` snare, `H` hi-hat | `S` |
| any | `---` stops the note; an empty cell lets it ring on | |

In the effect `0xy`, `x` and `y` are how many semitones above the note to add. They're written in
hexadecimal, so `C` means 12, an octave. `037` is a minor triad, `047` a major one, `038` a minor
triad in first inversion (the C chord in bar 3), `05C` a fourth plus an octave, and `07C` the
open fifth heard in a lot of game music. Arrow keys and Enter move around the grid. Click a cell and
play a note on MIDI or the on-screen keyboard to write that note in (Pulse 2 keeps its effect).
**Frames per arpeggio note** starts at 1 here, which is how trackers play `0xy`.

Some things to try:

- Change the chords: make bar 2 `F-4 037` (F minor) and hear the whole tune go darker.
- Give the triangle a walking bass line, a note every beat, instead of octaves.
- Write a drum fill in the last bar: an `S` on every row.
- Speed up to 3 frames per row and write a run of sixteenths that no one could play.

Your grid is kept in this browser. **Example tune** brings back the original, and **Clear** empties
everything.

## Music no one can play

Write that arpeggio out as sheet music and it isn't playable. At 150 bpm, a new note every two
frames is **12 notes per beat**: steady 48th-note triplets. A note every frame is 24 to a beat. The
fastest human trills and tremolos reach roughly 15 to 20 notes a second, and only on two notes, not
a chord broken note by note. A pianist playing a chip tune "as written" would need to play the
melody plus a chord broken into 30 notes a second in the other hand, perfectly even, for the
whole song.

Composers knew no one would ever play it. The parts were written for a machine, so the usual
limits of hands, breath and bows didn't apply. Some of them made a style of that:

- **Rob Hubbard** (*Monty on the Run*, 1985) and **Martin Galway** on the Commodore 64 wrote
  long, fast arpeggio passages and pitch slides that are part of the melody, not hidden behind it.
- **Tim Follin**'s NES music (*Silver Surfer*, 1990) has arpeggios, echoes and runs at speeds
  that sound like a much bigger chip.
- Fast single-note runs, octave leaps every frame, and drum fills on the noise channel quicker
  than any drummer are common.

Other tricks came from the same limits:

- **Echo**: pulse 2 plays the melody a few rows late and quieter, to sound like a delay
  ([Sound 17](sound-delay.qmd)) the chip didn't have.
- **Channel stealing**: a sound effect (a jump, a coin) takes over a pulse channel for a moment,
  and that part of the music drops out. Composers planned the music so that it still made sense
  with a part missing.
- **Pitch sweeps**: a note sliding down fast is a laser, or, on the triangle, a kick drum with
  more punch than noise alone gives.
- **Shared drums**: a quick noise hit and a triangle blip together, so a snare has a pitched body
  ([Sound 3](sound-noise.qmd) builds a snare the same way).

## Chiptune today

Many musicians still write for these chips, on the original machines or in trackers such as
FamiTracker and LSDj (which runs on a Game Boy). They follow the old limits on purpose: four
channels, frame timing, arpeggiated chords. A lot of the sound is the struggle with the limits.
Pop and electronic producers also use pulse waves and fast arpeggios, without the limits, when they
want that sound.
